explanation: A compact or small-screen layout can replace familiar labels, counters or a full grid with different controls. This pattern matches a report that concludes a function was removed because its usual desktop presentation is absent, although the reviewed layout still provides a working way to navigate dates, open records or select items. Identify and test the available alternative before alleging missing functionality. A task with no usable alternative, or essential content that remains unreadable, is a different failure.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and open Tasks. Create a uniquely named Calendar view and switch its calendar range to Day. Open the displayed date dropdown and observe month/year controls without selectable days. Use the picker month controls and the toolbar day arrows or Today; date navigation works. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation was that the Day toolbar dropdown provides selectable individual dates. It claimed this outcome: The dropdown shows only month/year controls and arrows. Day cells exist but are hidden, while month/year navigation, day-by-day toolbar arrows, and Today work. Review concluded: The header-only picker is intentional. Its Storybook scenario explicitly specifies a hidden calendar grid with only the month/year header. Day navigation remains available through working toolbar controls; no supported contract requires an individual-day grid in this dropdown.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace, set the viewport to 768px wide, and open a Tasks Table view. Confirm that task titles are readable before horizontal scrolling. Scroll the table horizontally to the right and observe that the first column compacts to initials. Scroll back left and confirm that titles return. Tap an initial to verify that it opens the corresponding task. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation was that readable task titles remain visible in the Title column at tablet width. It claimed this outcome: Titles are readable when the table opens. At widths up to 768px, horizontal scrolling deliberately hides title labels and compacts the first column to initials. Scrolling back restores titles and the initial remains clickable to open the task. Review concluded: The pinned fixture deliberately switches the first table column to compact initials while horizontally scrolled at widths up to 768px. Titles are readable on landing, scrolling back restores them, and tapping an initial opens the correct task. The landing-only missing-title claim did not reproduce. A later upstream change describes row-identification concerns and replaces compact mode, but that later design change does not make this deliberate, reversible behavior a bug in the fixture.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Select a Person in a mobile-width People table. Open the command menu and inspect or exercise selection-specific actions. The rejected report expected: Selection-specific commands should remain available in the mobile command menu; the desktop selection count need not be shown. It claimed this outcome: The mobile count is hidden, but Delete and Export remain available for selected People. Review concluded: Rejected by the user after independent review and a subsequent visual evidence audit. Missing mobile count is confirmed; claimed bulk-action dead end is false because visible Command Menu retains actions. Maintainer title-removal rationale is explicit. Both reviewers justified narrow functional rejection; do not claim all commands/touch tested. Reject the claimed bulk-action dead end, not a separately proven missing or inoperative command.

explanation: In Twenty, a relationship field links one record to another, such as assigning a record to an owner or company. When a list or board groups records by that relationship, the reviewed design displays the related-value groups the user explicitly configured, plus the unassigned group; it does not automatically add a group for every possible owner or company. This pattern matches a report of missing records caused solely by their related group not being included, when adding that group reveals the unchanged records. Missing records inside a configured group, broken group controls or actual deletion remain separate failures.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Open People and create a uniquely named Table view. Group the view by Company and observe that people with populated Company relations disappear from the initial groups. Choose New group and select a company that has linked people. Observe that those people reappear without editing their records. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation was that grouping by Company automatically displays every company group and preserves all visible people. It claimed this outcome: Only configured groups and the No Value group are shown initially. Adding a company through New group displays its people without changing their records. Review concluded: Relation groups are intentionally added explicitly through New group because a relation can have an unbounded number of groups. Both independent judges restored linked people by adding their company groups. Upstream PR #23619 explicitly documents this behavior as intended; its fixes concern changing or removing grouping, which is a separate defect.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace, open Companies, and create a uniquely named disposable Table view. Filter the view to Google and confirm the company is visible with count 1. Group the view by Account Owner and observe that Google disappears and the count becomes 0. Choose New group and select the owner assigned to Google. Observe that the unchanged Google record and count 1 return; reload and confirm the owner group persists. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation was that grouping by Account Owner automatically includes every owner group and preserves all matching companies. It claimed this outcome: Only configured owner groups and No Value are initially shown. Adding the matching owner through New group restores the same company and count without changing the record. Review concluded: Relation-backed groups are intentionally added explicitly through New group. Grouping by Account Owner initially includes only configured groups, so a company whose owner group has not been added is excluded from both rows and counts. Both independent judges restored the same unchanged records by adding the appropriate owner group, including after reload. Upstream PR #23619 documents this explicit relation-group design; this matches the rejected People/Company grouping finding N12.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and open /objects/companies. Create a uniquely named disposable view with Kanban layout. Observe only an empty No Value lane and zero record count. Choose Options > Layout > Table and confirm 599 companies with populated Account Owner values. Switch the same view back to Kanban and observe the missing company cards again. The rejected report expected: The Kanban layout displays companies grouped by Account Owner into lanes (including Jony Ive, Phil Schiller, and Tim Apple). It claimed this outcome: The Kanban layout displays only an empty 'No Value' lane with no company cards, despite the view containing 599 records. Review concluded: Companies Kanban intentionally starts with configured Account Owner groups and No Value. Both judges saw unowned companies, and adding owner groups restored the complete Table record set without company edits. The historical exact zero-versus-599 count is data-dependent and was not independently reproduced. Upstream PR #23619 explicitly preserves manual relation-group creation as intended behavior.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and open /objects/tasks. Create a uniquely named disposable Table view with no filters. Group by Status and sort Title descending, matching the reported setup. Confirm 1,800 tasks and populated Assignee cells. Choose Options > Group > Group by > Assignee. Observe the count change to zero and all task rows disappear. The rejected report expected: Existing tasks remain visible, grouped under their assignees; changing grouping should not filter all tasks out. It claimed this outcome: Count changes from 1,800 to 0 and all task rows disappear, leaving only an empty No Value group. Options > Group shows Assignee selected. Review concluded: Tasks Assignee grouping intentionally starts with explicitly configured groups and No Value. Adding the actual assignee groups restored the full task count without task edits, including after reload. A separately observed stale grouping-removal defect belongs to N18, not this initial omission. Upstream PR #23619 explicitly preserves manual relation-group creation as intended behavior.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and open /objects/people at 390px width. Create a uniquely named disposable Table view; filter Name Contains Mark, add a Name sort, and save. Confirm nine results. Switch to Calendar at 768px width. At 390px, switch to Day, navigate to the next day, then use Today. Confirm Mark cards appear. Choose Options > Layout > Kanban and dismiss the menu. Observe count zero and an empty No Value column. The rejected report expected: Kanban view should display the 9 matching records grouped by Company. It claimed this outcome: View count drops to 0 and only an empty 'No Value' column appears with no cards. Review concluded: People Kanban groups by Company and intentionally shows only configured company groups and No Value. Adding the matching companies through New group restored the filtered people without editing them. Saved-filter controls establish this intended grouping flow independently of pending-filter loss. Upstream PR #23619 explicitly preserves manual relation-group creation as intended behavior.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and open /objects/opportunities. Create a uniquely named disposable Kanban view with no filters. Add Amount descending, Count all summaries, and Hide empty groups to match the reported setup. Confirm 150 opportunities with populated Owner values. Open Options > Group > Group by and select Owner. Observe count zero and no opportunity cards or owner-named groups. The rejected report expected: Grouping the same unfiltered records by Owner should retain the 150 opportunities and display them under their owner groups. It claimed this outcome: The total changes from 150 to 0 and the board shows only an empty No Value column, without opportunity cards or owner-named groups. Review concluded: Opportunities Kanban Owner grouping intentionally shows only configured relation groups and No Value. Adding the appropriate owner through New group restored owned cards; Stage grouping retained all records as a control. The original literal zero count was not reproduced because the shared fixture also contained unowned opportunities. Upstream PR #23619 explicitly preserves manual relation-group creation as intended behavior.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and create a uniquely named Opportunities Table view. Apply Amount greater than or equal to 2,800,000. Confirm six rows: three iPhone Corporate records at $3.2m and three Mac Pro Rendering records at $2.8m. Choose Options > Group > Owner and dismiss the menu. Observe count zero, no opportunity rows or owner groups, and only column headers and New group. The rejected report expected: Grouping should partition the six matching rows into Owner groups, including unassigned rows, without excluding all records. It claimed this outcome: Six rows were visible before choosing Owner. Afterwards the table shows only column headers and New group, and count becomes 0. Review concluded: Opportunities Table Owner grouping intentionally includes only configured relation groups and No Value. Adding Tim Apple through New group restored all six matching owned opportunities without record edits. A separately reported failed grouping removal is N27, not this initial omission. Upstream PR #23619 explicitly preserves manual relation-group creation as intended behavior.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Filter an Opportunities board and group it by Company without configuring Company groups. Add the relevant Company groups and confirm the records become visible. The rejected report expected: Relation-based boards display records within explicitly configured relation groups. It claimed this outcome: Grouping by Company can initially hide records when no matching groups are configured. Adding Company groups restores the records. Review concluded: Rejected by the user after independent review and a subsequent visual evidence audit. Actual hide is confirmed but explicitly manual configured-group behavior supported by maintainer rationale PR23619/22123. Broad expectation auto-populate allCompanies unsupported. Source alone not basis. No recordloss; addgroup control recovers. Narrow rejection justified; do not reject separate accepted disabled-group controls. Reject automatic-group-population expectations, not record loss or the separately accepted disabled-group controls.

explanation: The report describes a failure, but independent review did not recover the claimed failing state under the stated conditions. This group records that evidence limitation rather than an established explanation of why the behavior was correct or why the original event occurred. A future report must match the same trigger and outcome and still needs its own reliable reproduction; resemblance to a nearby accepted bug is insufficient. Nonreproduction does not prove the event impossible or intended.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and open /objects/companies. Create a uniquely named disposable view and choose Options > Layout > Calendar. Confirm Month displays a dated grid. Change the calendar range dropdown from Month to Week. Observe that the toolbar remains but the entire calendar body disappears. For the responsive variants, repeat at 390px or 768px width in Tasks, Opportunities, or People. The rejected report expected: Week displays the days of the selected week in a usable calendar grid, even if there are no matching entries. It claimed this outcome: The Week selector and period navigation remain visible, but the body has no day/date columns, time grid, or record events. This is a missing calendar structure, rather than the seed issue that caps events on crowded dates. Review concluded: Both independent judges could not reproduce the reported blank Week body. Fresh Companies and Tasks views, other objects, desktop/tablet/mobile widths, empty weeks and reloads rendered dated Week grids. The original failing sandbox state is unavailable, so the cause of the historical Mo observation is unverified; this rejection does not establish that a blank calendar is intended.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and set the viewport to 390 × 844. Open /objects/people and create a uniquely named disposable Table view. Apply an advanced Name Contains Kimberly filter and save. Confirm five matching rows. Click the Select all header checkbox, then click the checked header checkbox again to deselect. Wait several seconds without further input and observe the rows revert to checked. The rejected report expected: Clicking the checked Select all checkbox deselects all visible rows and leaves them unchecked. It claimed this outcome: Clicking the checked Select all checkbox briefly unchecks the rows, but after several seconds they revert to checked. Review concluded: Both independent judges could not reproduce rows rechecking themselves after header deselection. Repeated mobile tests, including the exact five-People filter, prolonged waits and metadata updates, left all rows unchecked. A separately reproduced defect clears selected rows; that is the opposite behavior and does not validate this claim. The historical delayed recheck remains unverified, rather than proven impossible.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and create a uniquely named Companies Table view. Apply Name Contains micro and confirm MICROS Systems Inc, MicroStrategy, Microsoft and Microworkers. Select all four using the header checkbox. Click the checked Microsoft row checkbox. Confirm that Microsoft becomes unchecked while the other three remain selected and the header shows 3 selected. The rejected report expected: Microsoft becomes unchecked while the other three companies remain selected, showing 3 selected. It claimed this outcome: Both independent rechecks showed the expected selection: Microsoft unchecked, the other three checked and 3 selected. The reported state with only Microsoft selected did not reproduce. Review concluded: The reported inverted selection did not reproduce. Both independent judges repeatedly selected all four filtered companies and unchecked Microsoft; Microsoft became unchecked while the other three remained selected with count 3. Fresh views, saved and unsaved filters, the reported hidden-column/reload setup, different widths and input variations passed. The historical observation has no established cause and is not proven impossible; adjacent selection-clearing behavior does not validate this specific inversion claim.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: As an administrator, create two disposable Tasks and a fresh Status-grouped Kanban view, optionally filtering it to those tasks. Select a card and confirm the checked state and selected count. Open the top-right command menu and confirm the card remains checked, the count remains and task-specific commands appear. Repeat with the second task, Ctrl+K, reopening the menu, a settled reload and delayed checks. Compare a seeded Kanban or Table view. The rejected report expected: Opening the command menu preserves selected-task context and its selection-specific actions. It claimed this outcome: On fresh tasks and fresh or seeded Kanban views, both agents retained the checked card and selected count when opening the menu by mouse or Ctrl+K. The menu offered Delete Task and Export Task. Separate idle or unrelated-view-update selection clears were observed by Claude, but the menu trigger did not reproduce. Review concluded: Rejected by the user specifically for the reported Command Menu trigger, which neither independent judge reproduced across fresh data and controls. Adjacent selection loss does not validate this trigger. Accepted N37 remains an unrelated-view-rename selection defect. Claude’s API-rename variation is retained as separate evidence; it does not establish the historical Mo cause, a complete shared source chain or exact overlap. This rejection does not reject idle or metadata-triggered selection loss, nor assert the original event was impossible.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: In Tasks create a Calendar view with Date field Due Date. Use Month view for October 2026 and hover a Prepare meeting agenda card on October 30. Click its checkbox; repeat or focus it and press Space. Alternatively create a People Kanban view, add Google and Microsoft company groups, and click the checkbox on Mark Young's card. Compare with selecting a row in Table view. The rejected report expected: A card's checkbox should toggle to checked and select that record, exposing the selected-record count and applicable actions. It claimed this outcome: Checkboxes remain aria-checked=false after successful pointer clicks and Space, and no selected-record count/action state appears. Repeated clicks on People Kanban cards and Tasks Month calendar cards have no effect; Companies calendar checkboxes also failed. Table checkboxes correctly select records. Review concluded: Fresh Calendar, Tasks Kanban and People Kanban controls select successfully.

explanation: An interface can display an edit or newly created item before its background save, multi-step creation or notification processing has finished. This pattern matches reports that interrupt that unfinished work with a hard refresh, immediately run the previously saved configuration or check results before processing completes, then call the old state loss of a completed operation. Verify the actual completion and reread the same item or recipient. Acknowledged-save loss, ordinary navigation discarding valid edits, or an effect still absent after completion needs separate evidence.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in to the seeded Apple workspace and create a uniquely named People Table view. Apply an Emails filter matching an existing person, such as MARK.YOUNG@EXAMPLE.COM, and confirm the matching row. Choose the arrow beside Update view, select Create view, and create a uniquely named copy. Wait for creation to finish and for the copied view to become selected. Reload and reselect the copied view. Confirm that the email filter and matching record remain. The rejected report expected: A completed view copy preserves the current email filter and its matching records after reload and reselection. It claimed this outcome: Completed copies retain the email filter and matching record. In the original report, refresh occurred before creation finished and the old unfiltered base view reopened; the claimed initial filtered state of the new view was not shown. Interrupting the sequential creation requests can leave a partial copy without its filter. Review concluded: The reported loss after a completed Create view copy did not reproduce: both independent judges retained the email filter through reload and view reselection. Review of the original Mo recording found that refreshing interrupted the multi-request creation flow before the new view opened, returning to the old unfiltered base view. A deliberately interrupted creation can leave a partial view without filters, but that does not establish the reported completed-copy filter-loss claim.

In Twenty, follow this workflow: Open a People table, apply a filter and select Save as new view. Enter a unique name and click Create new view. Immediately refresh before creation finishes. Reopen the partial copy and observe missing fields or filters. A creation allowed to complete retains its fields and filters. The rejected report expected: Creation should save a complete view with its filters and fields, or roll back an interrupted creation. Reloading should not leave a permanent unusable saved view. It claimed this outcome: The named Table view persists but has zero visible fields and no copied filter, producing a blank record area and unfiltered total. A normal creation allowed to complete retains fields and filters. Review concluded: Explicitly rejected by the reviewer as reported: a deliberately interrupted multi-request creation flow is not an accepted bug for this benchmark. This does not reject a failure after completed view creation.

explanation: A report's specific factual claim is contradicted by a decisive observation or by a controlled repetition of the same setup. For example, the allegedly deleted value is still present, or the allegedly broken control performs the requested action when activated as described. Match this pattern only when that counterevidence addresses the same value, action and conditions; a vaguely similar successful workflow is insufficient. The finding rejects the checked allegation, not every related defect or every possible historical failure.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in and open Opportunities > By Stage. Create a fresh Kanban view grouped by Stage. Change grouping to Owner, then Company, then restore Stage. Choose Group > Sort > Reverse Alphabetical, refresh, and inspect all five stage headers. The rejected report expected: Stage column headers displaying stage names and amount totals should render above the Kanban columns after refresh. It claimed this outcome: Both independent judges retained stage labels after the reported grouping-change and reload sequence. The source Mo recording also retains stage labels above loaded cards at 00:18–00:20. Review concluded: The claimed disappearance was not reproduced in either independent investigation; both retained the stage labels on fresh views. The source Mo recording also visibly retains the labels. Placeholder aggregate dashes are distinct from missing stage headers. This does not establish that every historical header disappearance is impossible.

explanation: A list can sort a compound field, such as a person's full name, using several internal parts before applying the next explicitly selected sort. For example, the second part of the name may break ties before a later sort by another field gets a chance to apply. This pattern matches a report that calls the later sort ignored without testing records tied on every earlier component. Check the complete ordering rules and compare genuinely tied records before concluding that sort priority is broken.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in and open People in a table view. Sort Name by Last name and add Emails ascending as a secondary sort. Inspect people sharing a last name but having different first names; first name breaks the tie before Emails. As a control, create people with identical first and last names and distinct email addresses. Observe Emails sorts them correctly in both directions. The rejected report expected: The report expects Emails to break ties between equal last names before first names are considered. It claimed this outcome: Name sorting intentionally uses the other name component as its tie-breaker. Emails therefore applies only after both last name and first name tie. Both judges reproduced the reported appearance and verified that identical-full-name controls sort Emails correctly in both directions. Review concluded: This is intended full-name tie-breaking, explicitly specified by upstream PR #20445 and covered by pinned source tests. Both independent judges confirmed that Emails sorts correctly when both name components tie, and when Name sorting is removed.

explanation: A calendar record with a start time but no end time may still need a display duration. In the reviewed case the calendar supplies a one-hour duration, so a record starting shortly before midnight legitimately appears across two dates. This pattern matches a report that calls that one spanning record a duplicate solely because no end date was entered. Verify the record identity and actual interval; duplicate records, a wrong fallback duration or an ignored explicit end time are different failures.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in and create two test Opportunities with Close dates at 23:27 on distinct dates in the workspace time zone. Create a Calendar view using Close date as the start and None as the end date. Inspect Month and Week views. Observe that each late-night record spans its start date and the following day. As controls, use start times of 10:00, 22:30 and 23:00; these remain on one date. The rejected report expected: The report expects a record without a configured end date to appear only on its start date. It claimed this outcome: A Close date at 23:27 renders an interval through 00:27 on the following day. Independent browser controls reproduce the midnight overlap; earlier start times remain on one date. Review concluded: Intended fixture behavior: the date-time range utility and its tests explicitly assign a one-hour fallback when the end is missing or unusable. A 23:27 start therefore ends at 00:27 the next day. Upstream PR #22819 introduced this fallback; later PR #24868 simplified calendar configuration, which does not establish that the pinned behavior was a defect.

explanation: A paginated list reaches its end when there are no more distinct records to load, not when a particular familiar example appears. This pattern matches a report that calls the final row or Add New control an early cutoff without identifying a record missing from the complete current dataset. In the reviewed controls, the displayed final page agreed with whether another page existed. Compare record identities and the full result set under the same filters and sort; the position of seeded sample data is not a universal limit.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in and open the default unfiltered All People table. Note the current header total; the judged comparison had 1,215 People, including 15 retained test records. Scroll through the table in smaller increments until Abigail Scott and Add New appear at the bottom. Confirm intermediate scrolling continues to load rows normally and the terminal row agrees with the end of the current result set. The rejected report expected: The People table should load every record counted in its current result set. It claimed this outcome: Both independent investigations loaded all 1,215 current distinct records without gaps, including all 1,200 seeded People. Abigail Scott was the terminal record in the tested ordering, followed by Add New. The final page returned the remaining 75 records and hasNextPage false. Review concluded: No pagination cutoff or missing records was demonstrated. Both independent judges reached the same normal dataset end and verified 1,215 distinct loaded IDs with no gaps, including every seeded position from 1 through 1,200. The source seed places Abigail last in the tested ordering. The original complete 1,200-record network session was not re-audited; this rejection does not claim that Abigail must remain last under other sorts or later insertions.

explanation: A report about missing unassigned records must first establish that the tested records really have no owner. In the reviewed case, the sample records already belonged to an owner whose group was not included in the view. Their absence therefore did not demonstrate disappearance of unassigned records. Verify the saved owner and use a genuinely blank-owner control; uncertainty about earlier sample data cannot be replaced with an assumed precondition.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in and create or identify disposable Opportunities whose Owner field is actually blank. Create a fresh Opportunities Kanban view grouped by Stage and verify those records are present. Change Group by to Owner and observe the genuinely unowned records remain in No Value. Reload the view and confirm they remain visible. Add Tim Apple through New group. Observe Tim-owned records appear in a separate owner column while unowned records stay in No Value. The rejected report expected: Opportunities with no Owner should remain visible in the No Value group when grouping by Owner. It claimed this outcome: Both independent investigations retained genuinely unowned records in No Value across switching from Stage to Owner and reloading. Two fresh unowned records also stayed visible. Adding Tim Apple populated a separate owned-record column while No Value remained populated. The 150 seeded Opportunities were owned by Tim Apple, contrary to the report’s unowned-data premise. Review concluded: The specific unowned-row disappearance did not reproduce in either independent investigation, including fresh truly unowned controls. The 150 seeded records were owned by Tim Apple, so their omission before adding his configured group does not establish disappearance of unowned records. This rejection is limited to the unowned-row claim; it does not reverse earlier accepted or rejected labels about populated relation groups. The unavailable full historical recording and data state remain unverified.

explanation: A date-and-time filter compares records with a specific timestamp, which can include a visible editable time even when the user mainly selected a calendar date. It is different from a condition meaning the entire calendar day. This pattern matches a report that assumes the boundary is midnight and calls the results wrong while overlooking the time shown in the filter. Check the complete displayed timestamp and compare the records against it; a hidden time or a boundary applied differently from the visible choice is a different defect.
reproductionPaths: In Twenty, follow this workflow: Sign in as tim@apple.dev and open /objects/opportunities (All Opportunities table view). Filter > Close date, set operand 'Is', and pick Nov 21, 2026: 2 records (Close date Nov 21, 2026 10:49 AM). Change the operand to 'Is after or equal': count is 112, and the two Nov 21 records are missing. Change the operand to 'Is before': count is 38, and the two Nov 21 records are included. Compare: the API returns 114 for closeDate >= start of Nov 21 (PST) and 36 for < start of Nov 21. The rejected report expected: 'Is after or equal Nov 21' should include every record whose close date falls on or after Nov 21 (114 records, including the 2 that close Nov 21 at 10:49 AM). 'Is before Nov 21' should return only records before Nov 21 (36). It claimed this outcome: 'Is after or equal Nov 21' returns 112 and leaves out both Nov 21 opportunities (Enterprise iPad Deployment, Apple TV+ Enterprise License). 'Is before Nov 21' returns 38 and includes them. GraphQL filter: {closeDate:{gte:'2026-11-21T20:14:35.016Z'}} / {closeDate:{lt:'2026-11-21T20:14:35.016Z'}}. Review concluded: Editable time is visible in the chip; selecting midnight gives expected results.
